International Business Machines recently announced a series of quantum and AI moves, including new Nighthawk processors, a Chicago Quantum System Two deployment, multiple co-design platforms with partners such as NVIDIA, AMD, Fermilab, and Oak Ridge, and an AI agent platform collaboration with Microsoft.

These projects point to IBM leaning heavily into capital-intensive, research-heavy quantum and enterprise AI infrastructure. This could influence long-term margins, required investment, and how its Software, Consulting, and Infrastructure segments work together in practice.

The next area of focus will be how IBM's existing hybrid cloud and AI investment narrative aligns with its quantum co-design initiatives with NVIDIA.

Spot 53 AI infrastructure stocks that, like IBM, are pouring resources into quantum-ready AI hardware and enterprise platforms before this buildout phase matures.

International Business Machines Investment Narrative Recap

To own International Business Machines, you need to believe its shift toward hybrid cloud, AI and now quantum-ready infrastructure can keep earnings and cash flow resilient while growth stays moderate. Recent quantum and AI partnerships, plus the new Nighthawk roadmap, keep that thesis focused on Software and Consulting execution rather than one-off hardware wins.

The immediate catalyst is how quickly IBM converts its reported generative AI book of business into higher margin Software revenue and stable free cash flow. The recent yen fixed-income deals look incremental. They tweak funding and interest costs but do not materially change the near term risk, which still centers on high debt and execution in AI.

The IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 and r3 announcements look most relevant to this buildout. They sit right where the story is heading, toward quantum-ready AI infrastructure that leans on IBM Quantum Platform, classical supercomputing tie-ins, and a growing ecosystem across partners like Oak Ridge and AMD.

For you as a shareholder, the key issue is how effectively IBM turns that technical roadmap into commercial Software and Consulting projects that support margins while also funding capital-intensive quantum work. Execution on this front will likely matter more to the catalyst than funding mechanics. At the same time, the existing high debt load still depends on consistent free cash flow to remain manageable.

On kapirey's numbers, the narrative reaches a fair value of US$256.08 by applying a discounted cash flow style framework that assumes IBM can compound revenue at 6.0% a year and eventually sustain an 18.0% profit margin on that higher sales base.

title: IBM, Fermilab, and NVIDIA Announce Plans for New Co-Design Platform to Accelerate the Development of Next-Generation, Modular Quantum Computers
detail:

IBM, Fermilab, and NVIDIA Announce Plans for New Co-Design Platform to Accelerate the Development of Next-Generation, Modular Quantum Computers
CNW Group
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 10:00 AM CST 6 min read
IBM
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Researchers plan to use modular quantum computing co-design platform to explore computationally demanding problems in high-energy and nuclear physics.

New Slurm® integration simplifies how HPC users can orchestrate and manage quantum computing in their workflows.

Results from IBM, RIKEN, and NVIDIA demonstrate quantum-classical scientific simulations with 79 times more accuracy than previous work.

YORKTOWN HEIGHTS, N.Y., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- IBM (NYSE: IBM) today announced plans to collaborate with NVIDIA and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) to advance the integration of quantum and classical computing and explore how these technologies can scale together in the modular architectures that will define fault-tolerant quantum computers.

Conceptual hardware illustration of the combined strengths toward the new quantum co-design platform. IBM: quantum computers (pictured: IBM Quantum System Two; image credit: IBM). Fermilab/SQMS: ultracoherent superconducting cavities, prospective interconnects, quantum memories and bosonic resources (pictured: nine-cell SRF cavity; image credit: Ryan Postel, Fermilab). NVIDIA: accelerated computing platform (pictured: NVIDIA DGX B200; image credit: NVIDIA).

The work will span developing new scientific applications, integrating supercomputing and quantum resources, and designing critical components of future quantum computers. As part of the work, IBM and NVIDIA, together with Fermilab, intend to launch a modular quantum computing co-design platform that co-locates NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the most powerful quantum processor IBM has ever built, running circuits of up to 7500 two-qubit operations on 120 qubits with speeds up to 100,000 samples per second. Leveraging Fermilab's Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems (SQMS) Center, the SI-enabled co-design platform will help researchers explore and test the innovations needed for multiple quantum processors to work together to execute a large number of samples and scale classical compute alongside them.

Fermilab and IBM will also look to research what will be needed to execute complex calculations in high-energy and nuclear physics that are beyond the reach of classical systems alone, such as such as lattice gauge theories, neutrino interactions and nuclear simulations.

"Some of the most fundamental problems in science remain out of reach for classical computers alone. Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond," said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and Chief Technology Officer of Quantum-Centric Computing. "With Fermilab and NVIDIA, we plan to explore how these real-world problems can help us shape the modular, interconnected architectures that will define the next generation of quantum computers and accelerated classical computing."

"Realizing quantum computing's potential requires quantum processors and accelerated computing to evolve together as accelerated quantum supercomputers," said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at NVIDIA. "IBM, Fermilab, and NVIDIA are working together to give researchers the tools they need to make scientific discoveries with quantum computing."

IBM vs. Jabil: Which Stock is Better Positioned for AI Growth Now?

International Business Machines Corporation IBM and Jabil Inc. JBL are well poised to benefit from growing investments in AI and enterprise infrastructure. IBM offers cloud and data solutions that aid enterprises in digital transformation. In addition to hybrid cloud services and AI services, the company provides advanced information technology solutions, computer systems, quantum computing and supercomputing solutions, enterprise software, storage systems and microelectronics.

Jabil provides advanced manufacturing solutions for AI servers, data centers and networking infrastructure. It is one of the largest global suppliers of electronics manufacturing services (EMS) solutions. Jabil serves a diversified customer base in the aerospace, automotive, computing, consumer, defense, industrial, instrumentation, medical, networking, peripherals, storage and telecommunications industries.

Let us delve a little deeper into the companies' competitive dynamics to understand which of the two is relatively better placed in the industry to warrant a place in your investment portfolio.

The Case for IBM

IBM's growth is expected to be aided by analytics, cloud computing and security in the long term. With a surge in traditional cloud-native workloads and associated applications, along with a rise in generative AI deployment, there is a radical expansion in the number of cloud workloads that enterprises are currently managing. This has resulted in heterogeneous, dynamic and complex infrastructure strategies, which have led firms to undertake a cloud-agnostic and interoperable approach to highly secure multi-cloud management, translating into a healthy demand for IBM hybrid cloud solutions.

IBM has introduced a self-hosted deployment option for IBM Bob, its agentic software development platform. The move is aimed at helping enterprises adopt AI-powered software development and modernization tools while retaining greater control over sensitive data, source code and development environments. The offering can be deployed across on-premises, private-cloud, sovereign-cloud and air-gapped infrastructure, making it particularly relevant for organizations with stringent security, regulatory and data-residency requirements. By enabling customers to run supported AI models within controlled environments or connect to external models through hybrid configurations, IBM is seeking to address growing enterprise demand for secure and governed AI adoption.

Despite solid hybrid cloud and AI traction, IBM is facing stiff competition from Amazon.com, Inc.'s AMZN AWS and Microsoft Corporation's MSFT Azure. Increasing pricing pressure is eroding margins, and profitability has trended down over the years, barring occasional spikes. The company faces a potent threat from AI firm Anthropic as the latter's Claude Code tool can modernize legacy COBOL systems — a foundational programming language deeply embedded in IBM's mainframe ecosystem. With Claude Code proposing to substantially automate code exploration, documentation, refactoring and security analysis, it threatened to reduce enterprises' reliance on specialized legacy service providers like IBM, putting its sustenance at stake.

The AI market looks a little less invincible lately. After years of bull runs, semiconductor stocks came under pressure as investors started questioning whether all that spending will turn into actual profit. That, plus a run this long, has stretched valuations, so even a small disappointment can trigger an outsized selloff.

Because when the story is "growth at any price," a single wobble in sentiment can send valuations sharply lower.

More News from Barchart

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

For investors who still want exposure to technology without riding every swing, that's pushed attention toward a quieter corner of the sector: tech companies that pay dividends. A steady payout won't protect a stock from a selloff, but it does put money in your pocket while you wait for things to settle. It's also usually a sign of a mature business with real cash flow, not one that's banking on its next big funding story.

With that in mind, here are three Buy-rated tech stocks that pay solid dividends through thick and thin.

How I Came Up With These Stocks

Using Barchart's Stock Screener, I selected the following filters to get my list:

Screenshot courtesy of www.barchart.com

Market Sectors: Computers and Technology.

Annual Dividend Yield % (FWD): Set at 0.01% to filter for companies that pay a dividend. I'll sort the list later from highest to lowest yield.

Market Cap: $200 billion and up, which limits the list to "Mega" cap companies.

Number of Analysts: At least 16, because the more analysts covering a stock, the stronger the rating consensus.

Current Analyst Rating: 3.5 to 5, or stocks rated "Moderate" to "Strong Buy" by Wall Street analysts.

I ran the screen and got 21 results. I then arranged them from highest to lowest dividend yield, and will now cover the top three.

Screenshot courtesy of www.barchart.com

Kicking off this list is:

International Business Machines (IBM)
Screenshot courtesy of www.barchart.com

International Business Machines, better known as IBM, is one of the oldest names in enterprise technology. It's the company that likely made your first office computer tick. Today, IBM works more behind the scenes, providing the hybrid cloud software, consulting, and infrastructure that businesses and governments rely on. Artificial intelligence is also a growing part of that story, as IBM focuses on helping enterprises put AI to work inside the systems they already run, from data platforms to its mainframes.

With a market cap of about $233.5 billion, IBM is the smallest of the three on this list. However, it pays the highest dividend of the group, with a forward annual dividend of $6.76, translating to a yield of 2.76%. IBM has also raised its payout for 30 consecutive years, which puts it among the Dividend Aristocrats.

Based in Armonk, New York, International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) provides software, consulting, and infrastructure solutions. With a market capitalization of approximately $233.6 billion, the company helps businesses modernize operations, integrate artificial intelligence, manage hybrid cloud environments, and address complex technology challenges through enterprise platforms, services, and partnerships.

Shares of this technology giant have significantly underperformed the broader market over the past year. IBM has declined 18.9% during this period, while the broader S&P 500 Index ($SPX) has rallied nearly 10.1%. The trend has persisted in 2026, with the stock falling 16.6% year-to-date, compared with the index's 9.9% gain over the same period.

Likewise, IBM has substantially lagged the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), which has gained 18.8% over the past year and 18.3% year-to-date.

www.barchart.com

On Oct. 21, 2026, International Business Machines reported its third-quarter 2026 results, beating analyst estimates for both revenue and adjusted earnings. Revenue increased 4.7% year over year to $17.1 billion, while operating EPS rose 11% to $2.95. Software revenue grew 8% to $7.8 billion, led by 11% growth in Hybrid Cloud (Red Hat) and 19% growth in Data. Infrastructure revenue increased 4% to $3.7 billion, while Consulting revenue remained essentially flat at $5.3 billion. Following the earnings release, IBM shares rose 3.9%.

Looking ahead, IBM maintained its full-year 2026 constant-currency revenue growth forecast of 4% to 5%, while raising its free cash flow outlook to an increase of more than $1 billion year over year. The company also declared a quarterly dividend of $1.69 per share, payable on Dec. 10, 2026.

For the current fiscal year, ending in December 2026, analysts expect IBM's EPS to increase 7.2% to $12.42 on a diluted basis. The company has met or beaten the consensus EPS estimate in each of the last four quarters, which is impressive.

Among the 25 analysts covering IBM stock, the consensus is a "Moderate Buy." That's based on 11 "Strong Buys," two "Moderate Buys," eleven "Holds," and one "Strong Sell."
